headline: America masses troops around Iraq
text: The United States is moving its largest fighting force since the Gulf War of 1991 towards Iraq. About 65,000 American soldiers were in the Gulf region in early January, and the Pentagon wants more than 120,000 there within weeks; ships, aircraft and tanks are on their way. President Bush says Iraq is hiding weapons of mass destruction and must give them up or be disarmed by force.
imageCaption: M1 Abrams, 2024

headline: BMW builds its first Rolls-Royce
text: From 1 January only BMW may call cars 'Rolls-Royce'. Its new subsidiary Rolls-Royce Motor Cars, with a new plant at Goodwood in the south of England, is launching the Phantom saloon. Volkswagen keeps the old Crewe factory and the Bentley brand.
imageCaption: A Rolls-Royce Phantom built by BMW at Goodwood

headline: McDonald's first quarterly loss
text: McDonald's reported on 23 January charges of 810 million dollars in the fourth quarter of 2002 for restructuring, which led to its first quarterly loss since it went public in 1965. Jim Cantalupo is closing more than 700 restaurants, mostly in the US and Japan, and cutting 600 jobs.
imageCaption: A McDonald's restaurant with drive-thru

headline: Philip Morris Companies becomes Altria
text: The parent company of Philip Morris USA, Philip Morris International and Kraft Foods changed its name to Altria Group in January. The company says the name reflects that it is more than a cigarette maker; critics say it wants to escape the stigma of tobacco.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altria (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000095011703000291/ex99.txt (financial statements of Altria Group, formerly Philip Morris Companies, filed 29 January 2003, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Altria building, Richmond, Virginia
imageCredit: Eden, Janine and Jim from New York City

headline: Microsoft pays its first dividend
text: On 16 January Microsoft's board declared the company's first dividend, 16 cents a share for the year (8 cents after a two-for-one split also announced that day). For a company that has always kept its profits, it is a change of character.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/000103221003000121/d10q.htm (Microsoft 10-Q for the quarter to 31 December 2002, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Microsoft's campus in Redmond, Washington

headline: Profit falls to 11.5 billion in 2002
text: ExxonMobil reported on 30 January that its 2002 net income fell to 11.46 billion dollars from 15.32 billion in 2001, on revenue of 205 billion. Fourth-quarter profit, however, rose 53 percent to 4.09 billion.
imageCaption: ExxonMobil's refinery in Baton Rouge, Louisiana

headline: Millions march against a war in Iraq
text: The United States says Iraq is hiding weapons of mass destruction and must be disarmed by force. On 5 February Secretary of State Colin Powell laid out the American case before the UN Security Council, holding up a small vial to show how little anthrax it takes to kill. France, Russia, China and Germany were not convinced. On 15 February between 6 and 10 million people marched against a war in more than 600 cities; organisers counted about 3 million in Rome alone. Meanwhile the build-up goes on: by mid-February about 135,000 American soldiers are in the Gulf.
imageCaption: 15 February 2003 Iraq War protests, 2002
imageCredit: Users AK7, William M. Connolley on en.wikipedia

headline: Nikkei below 8,000, a fifth of its peak
text: The Nikkei fell to 7,862 on 11 March, about a fifth of its 1989 record, as war in Iraq loomed and worries grew about Japan's banks. Japan's economy has hardly grown in more than ten years and prices are falling. Since March 2001 the Bank of Japan has kept short-term rates close to zero and flooded the banks with money, a policy called quantitative easing, to fight the fall in prices.
imageCaption: A businessman in front of an electronic share board in Tokyo as the Nikkei opens lower, 11 March 2003
imageCredit: Photo by YOSHIKAZU TSUNO/AFP via Getty Images

headline: Alinghi wins the America's Cup for landlocked Switzerland
text: On 2 March the Geneva yacht Alinghi, owned by Ernesto Bertarelli and skippered by New Zealander Russell Coutts, won the America's Cup in Auckland, beating Team New Zealand five races to none. Switzerland, without a coastline, now holds sailing's oldest trophy.
imageCaption: The Swiss America's Cup yacht Alinghi under sail

headline: The US and Britain invade Iraq
text: After President Bush's ultimatum to Saddam Hussein expired, US-led forces invaded Iraq on 20 March, with British, Australian and Polish troops. The stated aim is to disarm Iraq of weapons of mass destruction, which UN inspectors had not found, and remove Saddam. France, Germany and Canada opposed the war, which the UN Security Council did not authorise. US crude, which had reached $37.87 a barrel on 12 March as war approached, fell to $27.18 by the 21st once the invasion began.
imageCaption: US Army officers at a command post during the invasion of Iraq, March 2003

headline: Illinois 'lights' verdict: 10.1 billion dollars and a 12 billion dollar bond
text: A judge in Madison County, Illinois, ordered Philip Morris USA to pay 10.1 billion dollars in a class action claiming that 'light' cigarettes were sold as less harmful, and to post a 12 billion dollar bond to appeal. The company says it cannot post a bond that large and may be unable to make its 2.6 billion dollar payment to the states due on 15 April. Altria shares lost about 22% in March.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764180/000119312503000925/dex991.htm (Philip Morris USA press release of 14 April 2003, which describes the March order; read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/mo.json
imageCaption: Madison County Courthouse, Edwardsville, Illinois

headline: Cisco buys Linksys and enters the home
text: Cisco is buying Linksys, a maker of inexpensive routers for homes and small offices with about 300 employees and more than $500 million in annual sales. It is Cisco's first move into consumer products.
imageCaption: A Linksys WRT54GS wireless router for homes

headline: Coca-Cola cuts another 1,000 jobs
text: Coca-Cola is cutting another 1,000 jobs, half of them at its Atlanta headquarters. Its carbonated drinks are growing slowly while juices, waters and teas grow fast, and Diet Coke with Lemon and Vanilla Coke, launched in 2001 and 2002, have been its main new products.
imageCaption: A can of Vanilla Coke

headline: DaimlerChrysler buys into Mitsubishi's truck business
text: On 14 March DaimlerChrysler bought 43% of Mitsubishi Fuso Truck and Bus, the truck business split off from Mitsubishi Motors in January. It adds a big Asian maker to DaimlerChrysler's truck business, which already includes Mercedes-Benz and Freightliner.
source: Mercedes-Benz Classic, Illustrated Chronicle 2003 ('Commercial vehicles: principal shareholder of Mitsubishi Fuso', 14 March 2003), https://mercedes-benz-publicarchive.com/marsClassic/en/instance/ko/2003.xhtml?oid=4913233 (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Head office of Mitsubishi Fuso Truck and Bus in Kawasaki, Japan

headline: Baghdad falls, and markets rally
text: US troops took Baghdad on 9 April, three weeks into the war. Iraqi oil fields were secured largely intact and the regime collapsed faster than feared. Oil prices have dropped and share prices have risen sharply. Better-than-expected company earnings added to the relief, and the S&P 500 rose 8% in April to 916.92.
imageCaption: A statue of Saddam Hussein comes down in Firdos Square, Baghdad, 9 April 2003

headline: Cantalupo's plan: fewer new restaurants, better existing ones
text: On 7 April Jim Cantalupo told investors that McDonald's will focus on selling more at existing restaurants instead of opening new ones. Capital spending in 2003 is cut to 1.2 billion dollars, 800 million less than in 2002, and the cash will go to paying down debt and to shareholders. From 2005 it targets systemwide sales growth of 3 to 5% and operating income growth of 6 to 7% a year. McDonald's shares gained about 18% in April, as the stock market rallied.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000104746903012415/a2107907zex-99.htm (release of 7 April 2003, read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/mcd.json
imageCaption: Big Mac, 2023

headline: Xstrata bids for Australia's MIM
text: On 7 April Xstrata agreed to buy MIM Holdings, the troubled Australian copper, zinc, lead and coal miner that owns the Mount Isa mines, for A$1.72 a share in cash, about US$3bn. The deal would more than double Xstrata's size and give it copper and coking coal for the first time. Xstrata plans to fund part of it by selling new shares to its existing investors.
imageCaption: The Mount Isa smelter complex, Queensland, Australia

headline: The iTunes Music Store opens
text: Apple opened the iTunes Music Store, where songs can be bought legally for download. For now it works only with Macs and in the United States.
imageCaption: The third-generation iPod, introduced in April 2003 alongside the iTunes Music Store

headline: New chips in production, market share up
text: On 8 May Nvidia reported revenue of 405 million dollars for the quarter to April, down from 583 million a year earlier, and a profit of 19.7 million. Chief executive Jen-Hsun Huang said its new GeForce FX family is in production across desktop, notebook and workstation chips and that its market share has risen; this month it also launched the faster FX 5900.
imageCaption: A GeForce FX 5900 graphics card, 2003

headline: Appeals court throws out the 145 billion dollar Engle verdict
text: In May Florida's Third District Court of Appeal overturned the 145 billion dollar Engle verdict. It ruled that the smokers were too different to be treated as one class, that the punitive damages were excessive, and that the plaintiffs' lawyers had used racially charged arguments to prejudice the jury. Altria shares gained about 34% in May.
imageCaption: Dade County Courthouse, Miami, Florida

headline: Canberra clears the MIM takeover
text: On 28 May Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said he would raise no objection under foreign investment policy to Xstrata's A$1.72-a-share bid for MIM, which values the company at A$4.9bn. MIM shareholders still have to vote; Xstrata's coal chief Peter Coates says MIM's board looked for alternatives and found none better. Metal prices firmed during the month as the Iraq war ended.
imageCaption: Lake Moondarra near Mount Isa, Queensland, Australia

headline: Berkshire buys Wal-Mart's distribution arm McLane
text: Berkshire agreed in May to buy McLane Company, the grocery distributor, from Wal-Mart. Berkshire keeps buying whole companies for cash: Shaw carpets, Johns Manville and Fruit of the Loom in the last two years.
imageCaption: McLane distribution trucks

headline: The Fed's rate falls to 1 percent
text: On 25 June the Fed cut its rate target by a quarter point to 1 percent, the lowest since the 1950s; since January 2001 it has cut thirteen times from 6.5 percent. Inflation is about 2.1 percent (May). The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 3.3 percent in June, the lowest since 1958, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 5.2 percent, the lowest since the mortgage company Freddie Mac began its weekly survey in 1971. The numbers: the Fed's rate 1.2 percent. Inflation 1.9 percent. Unemployment 6.1 percent.
imageCaption: The Fed's interest rate (blue), inflation (red) and unemployment (grey) in the United States, 1955 to June 2003
imageCredit: Chart: Month by Month. Data: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)

headline: US sales up 6.3% in May, the best in four years
text: McDonald's reported on 6 June that sales at US restaurants open at least 13 months rose 6.3% in May, the highest increase in four years, thanks to new premium salads, Happy Meal offers and better service. Worldwide comparable sales rose 2.2%. The shares gained about 18% in June.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000104746903020809/a2112576zex-99_2.htm (release of 6 June 2003, read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/mcd.json
imageCaption: A McDonald's drive-thru

headline: Federer wins Wimbledon
text: Roger Federer won Wimbledon in early July, beating Mark Philippoussis in the final after beating Andy Roddick in the semi-final. At 21 it is his first Grand Slam title and the first by a Swiss man.
imageCaption: Roger Federer holds the Wimbledon trophy after beating Mark Philippoussis in the final, 6 July 2003

headline: Chuck Prince to succeed Sandy Weill
text: Sanford Weill announced that Charles Prince, head of the corporate and investment bank, will become chief executive by 1 January 2004, with Robert Willumstad as chief operating officer; Weill stays chairman until the 2006 annual meeting. Citigroup also settled with the SEC, bank regulators and the Manhattan district attorney over its Enron dealings, paying $145 million.
imageCaption: Charles Prince of Citigroup

headline: Lehman buys Neuberger Berman for $2.6 billion
text: Lehman Brothers agreed to buy the fund manager Neuberger Berman for about $2.6 billion in cash and Lehman shares. The deal takes the assets Lehman manages for clients to more than $100 billion and makes it a leading firm for wealthy private investors.
imageCaption: Neuberger Berman, New York

headline: Heatwave: Switzerland passes 40 degrees for the first time
text: On 11 August Grono in the Misox valley measured 41.5 degrees, the first temperature above 40 ever recorded in Switzerland, beating the old record of 39 degrees from 1952. The summer of 2003 is the hottest on record across much of Europe, and in France thousands of old people have died in the heat.
imageCaption: Europe's summer 2003: temperature compared with the 1971-2000 average

headline: Schlumberger sells most of Sema to Atos Origin
text: On 22 September Schlumberger agreed to sell most of SchlumbergerSema to the French IT company Atos Origin for about 1.5 billion dollars: 400 million euros in cash and 19.3 million Atos shares, about 29 percent of the company. The company, led since February by chief executive Andrew Gould, says the sale strengthens its focus on oilfield services.
imageCaption: An Atos Origin office building, Atos Origin being the buyer of most of Sema

headline: Metals take off on Chinese demand
text: Base metal prices jumped in October: copper averaged $1,921 a tonne, up 7% from September and 20% from April; nickel rose to $11,047 from under $10,000 and zinc to $898. Coal is firming too. Xstrata, which now owns MIM's copper and zinc mines, is one of the most direct ways to ride the rise.
source: World Bank Commodity Price Data (Pink Sheet), monthly averages, CMO-Historical-Data-Monthly.xlsx updated 2026-10-02 (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: An open-pit copper mine: Bingham Canyon, Utah

headline: Sony to cut 20,000 jobs
text: Sony announced it will cut 20,000 jobs, 13% of its workforce, over three years to save about 3 billion dollars a year by 2006, and cut its operating profit forecast by 23%. It leads in plasma televisions but has only about 5% of the fast-growing LCD TV market.
imageCaption: A Sony Trinitron television

headline: China makes most of the world's DVD players
text: China produced about 30 million DVD players in 2002, nearly twice as many as the year before, and exported 20 million of them, up to 70% of the world market. A Chinese DVD player costs about 800 yuan, under $100. More than 100 Chinese companies make them, but they have paid 2.7 billion yuan, about $325 million, in royalties to the foreign owners of the patents, so China is now promoting its own disc format.
imageCaption: DVD player, 2025

headline: Roy E. Disney quits and starts a campaign against Eisner
text: Roy E. Disney, Walt Disney's nephew, resigned as chairman of Disney's animation division and from the board, and fellow director Stanley Gold resigned with him. The two set up a 'Save Disney' campaign to push out chief executive Michael Eisner.
imageCaption: Roy E. Disney, Walt Disney's nephew, 1990

headline: Cost cuts bring Siemens back to profit
text: On 13 November Siemens reported fourth-quarter net profit of 724 million euros, above expectations and up from 53 million a year earlier, as cost cutting paid off and the troubled telecom unit turned around. It forecast double-digit growth in net income for next year. The shares rose 2.8%.
imageCaption: Heinrich von Pierer, Siemens' chief executive, 1994

headline: 2003 in review: the bull returns, up 26 percent
text: The S&P 500 rose 26% in 2003 to 1,111.92, its first gain in four years, and the Dow 25.3% to 10,453.92. The Federal Reserve cut its key rate to 1 percent in June, and the end of major fighting in Iraq and rising profits brought investors back.
imageCaption: American shares (S&P 500) at the end of each month of 2003: up 26 percent in the year
imageCredit: Chart: Month by Month. Data: Yahoo Finance (^GSPC, month-end closes)

headline: Earthquake destroys the city of Bam
text: At dawn on 26 December an earthquake flattened the city of Bam in southeastern Iran, most of whose houses were built of mud brick. By the end of the month more than 25,000 bodies had been recovered and estimates of the dead ran as high as 40,000. The ancient citadel, Arg-e Bam, is largely destroyed. Rescue teams from dozens of countries arrived; the United States, which has no relations with Iran, sent aid and a rescue team.
imageCaption: The citadel of Bam, Iran, September 2003

headline: The Nasdaq gains 50% in 2003
text: The Nasdaq rose 50% in 2003 and closed the year just under 2,000, after briefly passing it on 29 December. The survivors of the bust, from Amazon to Nvidia, have multiplied from their lows.
imageCaption: The Nasdaq MarketSite on Times Square, New York, June 2003

headline: Chief executive Phil Condit resigns over the tanker scandal
text: On 1 December Boeing said chief executive Phil Condit has resigned; Harry Stonecipher, the former McDonnell Douglas chief, takes over. Boeing had fired its finance chief over the hiring of an Air Force procurement official who had worked on a deal to lease Boeing tankers, and the Pentagon has frozen the deal. Airbus is overtaking Boeing as the leading airliner maker this year.
imageCaption: Boeing chief executive Phil Condit

headline: Generics united under the Sandoz name
text: This year Novartis organised all its generic drug businesses into one division under the old name Sandoz.
imageCaption: The Sandoz and Hexal offices in Holzkirchen near Munich
